source: Hand-curated starter gazetteer; coordinates from the IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature. Integrity and Carroll are crew-proposed names whose locations are estimated from the crew's spoken directions.

places.name: Sea of Tranquility
places.fact: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed here on July 20, 1969. The dark 'seas' are old lava that cooled flat.

places.name: Aristarchus Plateau
places.fact: The brightest crater on the side we can see. The crew said the plateau looked like a yellow, snow-capped mountain.

places.name: Orientale Basin
places.fact: A giant bullseye 930 km wide, made by a huge impact. From Earth we only see its edge. Artemis II saw all of it.

places.name: Hertzsprung
places.fact: A huge crater with rings on the far side, the side that never faces Earth.

places.name: Vavilov
places.fact: A far-side crater with a mountain in the middle and walls stepped like stairs.

places.name: Ohm
places.fact: A young far-side crater with bright rays that spread out like a splash.

places.name: Glushko
places.fact: A bright young crater near the edge of the side we see, with long bright rays.

places.name: Reiner Gamma
places.fact: A bright swirl shaped like a tadpole. Scientists think a magnetic field keeps it from darkening.

places.name: Integrity
places.fact: The Artemis II crew proposed naming this crater after their Orion spacecraft, Integrity. They said it is halfway between Orientale and Ohm.

places.name: Carroll
places.fact: A bright spot the crew proposed naming Carroll, in memory of someone from their astronaut family. It's northwest of Glushko.

places.name: Tycho
places.fact: Tycho's bright rays stretch more than 1,500 km. At full Moon you can see them from Earth with binoculars.

places.name: Copernicus
places.fact: A big, sharp crater with terraced walls and mountains in the middle. Scientists call it the 'Monarch of the Moon.'

places.name: Sea of Rains
places.fact: Mare Imbrium, one of the biggest dark patches. It forms part of the 'face' people see in the Moon.

places.name: Sea of Crises
places.fact: A round dark sea near the Moon's right edge. It's easy to spot with your own eyes.

places.name: Shackleton (south pole)
places.fact: At the south pole, some crater floors never get sunlight, so ice may be hiding there. Artemis astronauts plan to land in this region.

places.name: Tsiolkovskiy
places.fact: A far-side crater with a dark, lava-filled floor and a bright mountain in the middle. It looks like an island in a sea.

places.name: South Pole–Aitken Basin
places.fact: One of the biggest impact craters in the solar system: about 2,500 km across, more than half as wide as the USA.

places.name: Grimaldi
places.fact: Grimaldi is a big, old crater about 173 km wide near the western edge of the side we see. It is named after Francesco Maria Grimaldi, an Italian astronomer.

places.name: Kepler
places.fact: Kepler is a crater about 29 km wide on the side of the Moon we see. It is named after Johannes Kepler, the German astronomer who worked out how planets move.

places.name: Byrgius A
places.fact: Byrgius A is a small crater about 18 km wide near the western edge of the side we see. It is a little neighbor of the crater Byrgius, named after Joost Bürgi, a Swiss clockmaker.

places.name: Pythagoras
places.fact: Pythagoras is a crater about 145 km wide, far in the north near the edge of the side we see. It is named after Pythagoras, the Greek mathematician.

places.name: Mare Humorum
places.fact: Mare Humorum, the Sea of Moisture, is a dark lava plain about 420 km wide on the side of the Moon we see. There is no water in it; the dark seas are old lava that cooled flat.

places.name: North Pole
places.fact: This is the Moon's north pole, the very top of the Moon at 90 degrees north. Near the poles the Sun stays low in the sky, so long shadows stretch across the ground.
